entries.0cf4dc1bc948f60de83ce9f0d6b9aea6f4152925: <div sID="gen24386" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Mark.3" sID="Mark.3"/> <div eID="gen24386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24387" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24388" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, we have, I. Christ's healing a man that had a withered hand, on the sabbath day, and the combination of his enemies against him for it, <reference osisRef="Mark.3.1-Mark.3.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. The universal resort of people to him from all parts, to be healed, and the relief they all found with him, <reference osisRef="Mark.3.7-Mark.3.12">ver. 7-12</reference>. III. His ordaining his twelve apostles to be attendants on him, and the preachers of his gospel, <reference osisRef="Mark.3.13-Mark.3.21">ver. 13-21</reference>. IV. His answer to the blasphemous cavils of the scribes, who imputed his power to cast out devils to a confederacy with the prince of the devils, <reference osisRef="Mark.3.22-Mark.3.30">ver. 22-30</reference>. V. His owning his disciples for his nearest and dearest relations, <reference osisRef="Mark.3.31-Mark.3.35">ver. 31-35</reference>.
entries.41ef318171a39baaaaae30cdf6849b6a51575867: <div eID="gen24388" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24387" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Withered Hand Restored; Multitudes Healed.</title> <div sID="gen24389" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And he entered again into the synagogue; and there was a man there which had a withered hand. <hi type="super">2</hi> And they watched him, whether he would heal him on the sabbath day; that they might accuse him. <hi type="super">3</hi> And he saith unto the man which had the withered hand, Stand forth. <hi type="super">4</hi> And he saith unto them, Is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days, or to do evil? to save life, or to kill? But they held their peace. <hi type="super">5</hi> And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched <hi type="italic">it</hi> out: and his hand was restored whole as the other. <hi type="super">6</hi> And the Pharisees went forth, and straightway took counsel with the Herodians against him, how they might destroy him. <hi type="super">7</hi> But Jesus withdrew himself with his disciples to the sea: and a great multitude from Galilee followed him, and from Judæa, <hi type="super">8</hi> And from Jerusalem, and from Idumæa, and <hi type="italic">from</hi> beyond Jordan; and they about Tyre and Sidon, a great multitude, when they had heard what great things he did, came unto him. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he spake to his disciples, that a small ship should wait on him because of the multitude, lest they should throng him. <hi type="super">10</hi> For he had healed many; insomuch that they pressed upon him for to touch him, as many as had plagues. 11 And unclean spirits, when they saw him, fell down before him, and cried, saying, Thou art the Son of God. <hi type="super">12</hi> And he straitly charged them that they should not make him known. <div eID="gen24389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24390" type="x-p"/> Here, as before, we have our Lord Jesus busy at work <hi type="italic">in the synagogue</hi> first, and then by <hi type="italic">the sea side;</hi> to teach us that his presence should not be confined either to the one or to the other, but, wherever any are gathered together in his name, whether <hi type="italic">in the synagogue</hi> or any where else, there is he in the midst of them. <hi type="italic">In every place where he records his name,</hi> he will meet his people, and <hi type="italic">bless them;</hi> it is his will that men <hi type="italic">pray every where.</hi> Now here we have some account of what he did. <div eID="gen24390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24391" type="x-p"/> I. When he <hi type="italic">entered again into the synagogue,</hi> he improved the opportunity he had there, of doing good, and having, no doubt, preached a sermon there, he wrought a miracle for the confirmation of it, or at least for the confirmation of this truth—that <hi type="italic">it is lawful to do good on the sabbath day.</hi> We had the narrative, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.9">Matt. xii. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen24391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24392" type="x-p"/> 1. The patient's case was piteous; he had a <hi type="italic">withered hand,</hi> by which he was disabled to work for his living; and those that are so, are the most proper objects of charity; let those be helped that cannot help themselves. <div eID="gen24392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24393" type="x-p"/> 2. The spectators were very unkind, both to the patient and to the Physician; instead of interceding for a poor neighbour, they did what they could to hinder his cure: for they intimated that if Christ cured him now on the sabbath day, they would accuse him as a <hi type="italic">Sabbath breaker.</hi> It had been very unreasonable, if they should have opposed a physician or surgeon in helping any poor body in misery, by ordinary methods; but much more absurd was it to oppose him that cured without any labour, but by a word's speaking. <div eID="gen24393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24394" type="x-p"/> 3. Christ dealt very fairly with the spectators, and dealt with them <hi type="italic">first,</hi> if possible to <hi type="italic">prevent</hi> the offence. <div eID="gen24394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24395" type="x-p"/> (1.) He laboured to convince their judgment. He bade the man <hi type="italic">stand forth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.3">v. 3</reference>), that by the sight of him they might be moved with compassion toward him, and might not, for shame, account his cure a crime. And then he appeals to their own consciences; though the thing <hi type="italic">speaks itself,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">he</hi> is pleased to <hi type="italic">speak</hi> it; "<hi type="italic">Is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days,</hi> as I design to do, <hi type="italic">or to do evil,</hi> as you design to do? Whether is better, to <hi type="italic">save life</hi> or to <hi type="italic">kill?</hi>" What fairer question could be put? And yet, because they saw it would turn against them, <hi type="italic">they held their peace.</hi> Note, Those are obstinate indeed in their infidelity, who, when they can say nothing <hi type="italic">against</hi> a truth, will say nothing <hi type="italic">to it;</hi> and, when they cannot <hi type="italic">resist,</hi> yet will not <hi type="italic">yield.</hi> <div eID="gen24395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24396" type="x-p"/> (2.) When they rebelled against the light, he <hi type="italic">lamented their stubbornness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.5">v. 5</reference>); <hi type="italic">He looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts.</hi> The <hi type="italic">sin</hi> he had an eye to, was, the <hi type="italic">hardness of their hearts,</hi> their insensibleness of the evidence of his miracles, and their inflexible resolution to persist in unbelief. We hear what is said amiss, and see what is done amiss; but Christ looks at the <hi type="italic">root of bitterness</hi> in the heart, the blindness and hardness of <hi type="italic">that.</hi> Observe, [1.] How he was <hi type="italic">provoked</hi> by the sin; he looked <hi type="italic">round upon them;</hi> for they were so many, and had so placed themselves, that they surrounded him: and he looked <hi type="italic">with anger;</hi> his anger, it is probable, appeared in his countenance; his anger was, like God's, without the least <hi type="italic">perturbation</hi> to himself, but not without great <hi type="italic">provocation</hi> from us. Note, The sin of sinners is very displeasing to Jesus Christ; and the way to be angry, and not to sin, is it be angry, as Christ was, at nothing but sin. Let hard-hearted sinners tremble to think of the anger with which he will <hi type="italic">look round</hi> upon them shortly, when the <hi type="italic">great day of his wrath comes.</hi> [2.] How he <hi type="italic">pitied</hi> the sinners; he was <hi type="italic">grieved for the hardness of their hearts;</hi> as God was grieved forty years for the hardness of the hearts of their fathers in the wilderness. Note, It is a great grief to our Lord Jesus, to see sinners bent upon their own ruin, and obstinately set against the methods of their conviction and recovery, for he would not that any should perish. This is a good reason why the hardness of our own hearts and of the hearts of others, should be a grief to us. <div eID="gen24396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24397" type="x-p"/> 4. Christ dealt very kindly with the patient; he bade him <hi type="italic">stretch forth his hand,</hi> and it was immediately <hi type="italic">restored.</hi> Now, (1.) Christ has hereby taught us to go on with resolution in the way of our duty, how violent soever the opposition is, that we meet with in it. We must deny ourselves sometimes in our ease, pleasure, and convenience, rather than give offence even to those who causelessly take it; but we must not deny ourselves the satisfaction of serving God, and doing good, though offence may unjustly be taken at it. None could be more tender of giving offence than Christ; yet, rather than send this poor man away uncured, he would venture offending all the scribes and Pharisees that compassed him about. (2.) He hath hereby given us a <hi type="italic">specimen</hi> of the cures wrought by his grace upon <hi type="italic">poor souls;</hi> our hands are spiritually <hi type="italic">withered,</hi> the powers of our souls weakened by sin, and disabled for that which is good. The great healing day is the <hi type="italic">sabbath,</hi> and the healing place the <hi type="italic">synagogue;</hi> the healing power is that of Christ. The gospel command is like this recorded here; and the command is rational and just; though our hands are withered, and we cannot of ourselves <hi type="italic">stretch them forth,</hi> we must attempt it, must, as well as we can, <hi type="italic">lift them up</hi> to God in prayer, <hi type="italic">lay hold</hi> on Christ and eternal life, and employ them in good works; and if we do our endeavour, power goes along with the word of Christ, he effects the cure. Though our hands be <hi type="italic">withered,</hi> yet, if we will not offer to <hi type="italic">stretch them out,</hi> it is our own fault that we are not healed; but if we do, and are healed, Christ and his power and grace must have all the glory. <div eID="gen24397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24398" type="x-p"/> 5. The enemies of Christ dealt very barbarously with him. Such a work of <hi type="italic">mercy</hi> should have engaged their love <hi type="italic">to him,</hi> and such a work of <hi type="italic">wonder</hi> their faith <hi type="italic">in him.</hi> But, instead of that, the Pharisees, who pretended to be oracles in the church, and the Herodians, who pretended to be the supporters of the state, though of opposite interests one to another, <hi type="italic">took counsel together against him, how they might destroy him.</hi> Note, They that suffer for doing good, do but suffer as their Master did. <div eID="gen24398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24399" type="x-p"/> II. When he withdrew <hi type="italic">to the sea,</hi> he did good there. While his enemies sought to <hi type="italic">destroy him,</hi> he quitted the place; to teach us in troublous times to shift for our own safety; but see here, <div eID="gen24399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24400" type="x-p"/> 1. How he was followed into his retirement. When some had such an enmity to him, that they drove him out of their country, others had such a value for him, that they followed him wherever he went; and the enmity of their leaders to Christ did not cool their respect to him. <hi type="italic">Great multitudes</hi> followed him from all parts of the nation; as far north, as <hi type="italic">from Galilee;</hi> as far south, as from Judea and Jerusalem; nay, and from Idumea; as far east, as from beyond Jordan; and west, as from about Tyre and Sidon, <reference osisRef="Mark.3.7-Mark.3.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. Observe, (1.) What induced them to follow him; it was the report they heard of the <hi type="italic">great things he did</hi> for all that applied themselves to him; some wished <hi type="italic">to see</hi> one that had done such <hi type="italic">great things,</hi> and others hoped he would do great things <hi type="italic">for them.</hi> Note, The consideration of the <hi type="italic">great things</hi> Christ has done, should engage us to <hi type="italic">come to him.</hi> (2.) What they followed him for (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.10">v. 10</reference>); They <hi type="italic">pressed upon him, to touch him, as many as had plagues.</hi> Diseases are here called <hi type="italic">plagues,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">mastigas</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">corrections, chastisements;</hi> so they are designed to be, to make us <hi type="italic">smart</hi> for our sins, that thereby we may be made <hi type="italic">sorry</hi> for them, and may be warned not to return to them. Those that were under these <hi type="italic">scourgings</hi> came to Jesus; this is the errand on which sickness is sent, to quicken us to enquire after Christ, and apply ourselves to him as our Physician. They <hi type="italic">pressed upon him,</hi> each striving which should get <hi type="italic">nearest to</hi> him, and which should be <hi type="italic">first served.</hi> They <hi type="italic">fell down before him</hi> (so Dr. Hammond), as petitioners for his favour; they desired leave but to <hi type="italic">touch him,</hi> having faith to be healed, not only by <hi type="italic">his</hi> touching <hi type="italic">them,</hi> but by <hi type="italic">their</hi> touching him; which no doubt they had many instances of. (3.) What provision he made to be ready to attend them (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.9">v. 9</reference>); He <hi type="italic">spoke to his disciples,</hi> who were fishermen, and had fisher-boats at command, that a <hi type="italic">small ship should</hi> constantly <hi type="italic">wait on him,</hi> to carry him from place to place on the same coast; that, when he had despatched the necessary business he had to do in one place, he might easily remove to another, where his presence was requisite, without pressing through the crowds of people that followed him for curiosity. Wise men, as much as they can, decline a crowd. <div eID="gen24400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24401" type="x-p"/> 2. What abundance of good he did in his retirement. He did not withdraw to be idle, nor did he send back those who rudely crowded after him when he withdrew, but took it kindly, and gave them what they came for; for he never said to any that sought him diligently, <hi type="italic">Seek ye me in vain.</hi> (1.) Diseases were effectually cured; He <hi type="italic">healed many;</hi> divers sorts of patients, ill of divers sorts of diseases; though numerous, though various, he <hi type="italic">healed them.</hi> (2.) <hi type="italic">Devils</hi> were effectually <hi type="italic">conquered;</hi> those whom unclean spirits had got possession of, <hi type="italic">when they saw him,</hi> trembled at his presence, and they also <hi type="italic">fell down before him,</hi> not to supplicate his favour, but to deprecate his wrath, and by their own terrors were compelled to own that <hi type="italic">he was the Son of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.3.1">v. 1</reference>. It is sad that this great truth should be denied by any of the children of men, who may have the benefit of it, when a confession of it has so often been extorted from devils, who are excluded from having benefit by it. (3.) Christ sought not applause to himself in doing those great things, for <hi type="italic">he strictly charged</hi> those for whom he did them, <hi type="italic">that they should not make him known</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.12">v. 12</reference>); that they should not be <hi type="italic">industrious</hi> to spread the notice of his cures, as it were by advertisements in the newspapers, but let them leave <hi type="italic">his own works to praise him,</hi> and let the report of them <hi type="italic">diffuse itself,</hi> and make its own way. Let not those that are cured, be forward to divulge it, lest it should feed their pride who are so <hi type="italic">highly favoured;</hi> but let the <hi type="italic">standers-by</hi> carry away the intelligence of it. When we do that which is <hi type="italic">praiseworthy,</hi> and yet covet not to be <hi type="italic">praised of men</hi> for it, then <hi type="italic">the same mind is in us,</hi> which was <hi type="italic">in Christ Jesus.</hi>
entries.7022869831e8550e5f6247b6c155fa2790eaeaa1: <div eID="gen24401" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Calling of the Apostles.</title> <div sID="gen24402" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> And he goeth up into a mountain, and calleth <hi type="italic">unto him</hi> whom he would: and they came unto him. <hi type="super">14</hi> And he ordained twelve, that they should be with him, and that he might send them forth to preach, <hi type="super">15</hi> And to have power to heal sicknesses, and to cast out devils: <hi type="super">16</hi> And Simon he surnamed Peter; <hi type="super">17</hi> And James the <hi type="italic">son</hi> of Zebedee, and John the brother of James; and he surnamed them Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder: <hi type="super">18</hi> And Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the <hi type="italic">son</hi> of Alphæus, and Thaddæus, and Simon the Canaanite, <hi type="super">19</hi> And Judas Iscariot, which also betrayed him: and they went into a house. 20 And the multitude cometh together again, so that they could not so much as eat bread. <hi type="super">21</hi> And when his friends heard <hi type="italic">of it,</hi> they went out to lay hold on him: for they said, He is beside himself. <div eID="gen24402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24403" type="x-p"/> In these verses, we have, <div eID="gen24403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24404" type="x-p"/> I. The choice Christ made of the <hi type="italic">twelve apostles</hi> to be his constant followers and attendants, and to be sent abroad as there was occasion, to preach the gospel. Observe, <div eID="gen24404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24405" type="x-p"/> 1. The introduction to this <hi type="italic">call</hi> or <hi type="italic">promotion</hi> of disciples; He <hi type="italic">goes up into a mountain,</hi> and his errand thither was <hi type="italic">to pray.</hi> Ministers must be set apart with solemn prayer for the pouring out of the Spirit upon them; though Christ had authority to confer the gifts of the Holy Ghost, yet, to set us an example, he prayed for them. <div eID="gen24405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24406" type="x-p"/> 2. The rule he went by in his choice, and that was his own good pleasure; <hi type="italic">He called unto him whom he would.</hi> Not such as we should have thought <hi type="italic">fittest to be called, looking upon the countenance, and the height of the stature;</hi> but such as he <hi type="italic">thought fit</hi> to call, and determined to <hi type="italic">make fit</hi> for the service to which he called them: <hi type="italic">even so,</hi> blessed Jesus, <hi type="italic">because it seemed good in thine eyes.</hi> Christ calls <hi type="italic">whom he will;</hi> for he is a free Agent, and his grace is his own. <div eID="gen24406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24407" type="x-p"/> 3. The efficacy of the call; He <hi type="italic">called them</hi> to separate themselves from the crowd, and stand by him, and they <hi type="italic">came unto him.</hi> Christ calls those who were <hi type="italic">given him</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.6">John xvii. 6</reference>); and <hi type="italic">all that the Father gave him, shall come to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.37">John vi. 37</reference>. Those whom it was his <hi type="italic">will</hi> to call, he made <hi type="italic">willing to come;</hi> his <hi type="italic">people shall be willing in the day of his power.</hi> Perhaps they came to him readily enough, because they were in expectation of <hi type="italic">reigning with him</hi> in temporal pomp and power; but when afterward they were <hi type="italic">undeceived</hi> in that matter, yet they had such a prospect given them of better things, that they would not say they were <hi type="italic">deceived</hi> in their Master, nor repented their leaving all to be with him. <div eID="gen24407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24408" type="x-p"/> 4. The end and intention of this call; He <hi type="italic">ordained them</hi> (probably by the imposition of hands, which was a ceremony used among the Jews), <hi type="italic">that they should be with him</hi> constantly, to be witnesses of <hi type="italic">his doctrine, manner of life, and patience,</hi> that they might <hi type="italic">fully know it,</hi> and be able to give an account of it; and especially that they might attest the truth of his miracles; they must be <hi type="italic">with him</hi> to receive instructions <hi type="italic">from him,</hi> that they might be qualified to give instructions <hi type="italic">to others.</hi> It would <hi type="italic">require time</hi> to fit them for that which he designed them for; for they must be <hi type="italic">sent forth to preach;</hi> not to preach till they were <hi type="italic">sent,</hi> and not to be <hi type="italic">sent</hi> till by a long and intimate acquaintance with Christ they were fitted. Note, Christ's ministers must be much <hi type="italic">with him.</hi> <div eID="gen24408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24409" type="x-p"/> 5. The power he gave them to work miracles; and hereby he put a very great honour upon them, beyond that of the great men of the earth. He ordained them to <hi type="italic">heal sicknesses and to cast out devils.</hi> This showed that the power which Christ had to work these miracles was an <hi type="italic">original</hi> power; that he had it not <hi type="italic">as a Servant,</hi> but <hi type="italic">as a Son in his own house,</hi> in that he could confer it upon others, and invest them with it: they have a rule in the law, <hi type="italic">Deputatus non potest deputare—He that is only deputed himself, cannot depute another;</hi> but our Lord Jesus had <hi type="italic">life in himself,</hi> and the Spirit without measure; for he could give this power even to the <hi type="italic">weak</hi> and <hi type="italic">foolish things</hi> of the world. <div eID="gen24409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24410" type="x-p"/> 6. Their number and names; He <hi type="italic">ordained twelve,</hi> according to the number of the twelve tribes of Israel. They are here named not just in the same order as they were in Matthew, nor by couples, as they were there; but as there, so here, Peter is put first and Judas last. Here Matthew is put before Thomas, probably being called in that order; but in that catalogue which Matthew himself drew up, he puts himself after Thomas; so far was he from insisting upon the precedency of his consecration. But that which Mark only takes notice of in this list of the apostles, is, that Christ called James and John <hi type="italic">Boanerges,</hi> which is, <hi type="italic">The sons of thunder;</hi> perhaps they were remarkable for a loud commanding voice, they were thundering preachers; or, rather, it denotes the zeal and fervency of their spirits, which would make them active for God above their brethren. These two (saith Dr. Hammond) were to be special eminent ministers of the gospel, which is called <hi type="italic">a voice shaking the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.26">Heb. xii. 26</reference>. Yet John, one of those <hi type="italic">sons of thunder,</hi> was full of love and tenderness, as appears by his epistles, and was the beloved disciple. <div eID="gen24410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24411" type="x-p"/> 7. Their retirement with their Master, and close adherence to him; <hi type="italic">They went into a house.</hi> Now that this jury was impanelled, they <hi type="italic">stood together, to hearken to their evidence.</hi> They went together into the house, to settle the orders of their infant college; and now, it is likely, the bag was given to Judas, which pleased him, and made him easy. <div eID="gen24411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24412" type="x-p"/> II. The continual crowds that attended Christ's motions (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.20">v. 20</reference>); The <hi type="italic">multitude cometh together again,</hi> unsent for, and unseasonably pressing upon him, some with one errand and some with another; so that he and his disciples could not get time <hi type="italic">so much as to eat bread,</hi> much less for a set and full meal. Yet he did not shut his doors against the petitioners, but bade them welcome, and gave to each of them <hi type="italic">an answer of peace.</hi> Note, They whose hearts are enlarged in the work of God, can easily bear with great inconveniences to themselves, in the prosecution of it, and will rather lose a meal's meat at any time than slip an opportunity of doing good. It is happy when zealous <hi type="italic">hearers</hi> and zealous <hi type="italic">preachers</hi> thus <hi type="italic">meet,</hi> and encourage one another. Now the <hi type="italic">kingdom of God was preached,</hi> and men pressed into it, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.16">Luke xvi. 16</reference>. This was a gale of opportunity worth improving; and the disciples might well afford to adjourn their meals, to lay hold on it. It is good striking while the iron is hot. <div eID="gen24412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24413" type="x-p"/> III. The care of his relations concerning him (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.21">v. 21</reference>); <hi type="italic">When his friends</hi> in Capernaum heard how he was followed, and what pains he took, they <hi type="italic">went out, to lay hold on him,</hi> and fetch him home, for they said, <hi type="italic">He is beside himself.</hi> 1. Some understand it of an absurd preposterous care, which had more in it of reproach to him than of respect; and so we must take it as we read it, <hi type="italic">He is beside himself;</hi> either they suspected it themselves, or it was suggested to them, and they gave credit to the suggestion, that he was <hi type="italic">gone distracted,</hi> and therefore his friends ought to bind him, and put him in a dark room, to bring him to his right mind again. His kindred, many of them, had mean thoughts of him (<reference osisRef="John.7.5">John vii. 5</reference>), and were willing to hearken to this ill construction which some put upon his great zeal, and to conclude him crazed in his intellects, and under that pretence to take him off from his work. The prophets were called <hi type="italic">mad fellows,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.11">2 Kings ix. 11</reference>. 2. Others understand it of a <hi type="italic">well-meaning</hi> care; and then they read <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">exeste</hi></hi>—"<hi type="italic">He fainteth,</hi> he has no time to <hi type="italic">eat bread,</hi> and therefore his strength will fail him; he will be stifled with the crowd of people, and will have his spirits quite exhausted with constant speaking, and the virtue that <hi type="italic">goes out of him</hi> in his miracles; and therefore let us use a friendly violence with him, and get him a little <hi type="italic">breathing-time.</hi>" In his preaching-work, as well as his suffering-work, he was attacked with, <hi type="italic">Master, spare thyself.</hi> Note, They who go on with vigour and zeal in the work of God, must expect to meet with hindrances, both from the groundless disaffection of their enemies, and the mistaken affections of their friends, and they have need to stand upon their guard against both.
entries.107b356c02f74900ab02a5335f7772d3b1c26036: <div eID="gen24413" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Blasphemy of the Scribes.</title> <div sID="gen24414" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> And the scribes which came down from Jerusalem said, He hath Beelzebub, and by the prince of the devils casteth he out devils. <hi type="super">23</hi> And he called them <hi type="italic">unto him,</hi> and said unto them in parables, How can Satan cast out Satan? <hi type="super">24</hi> And if a kingdom be divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. <hi type="super">25</hi> And if a house be divided against itself, that house cannot stand. <hi type="super">26</hi> And if Satan rise up against himself, and be divided, he cannot stand, but hath an end. 27 No man can enter into a strong man's house, and spoil his goods, except he will first bind the strong man; and then he will spoil his house. <hi type="super">28</hi> Verily I say unto you, All sins shall be forgiven unto the sons of men, and blasphemies wherewith soever they shall blaspheme: <hi type="super">29</hi> But he that shall blaspheme against the Holy Ghost hath never forgiveness, but is in danger of eternal damnation: <hi type="super">30</hi> Because they said, He hath an unclean spirit. <div eID="gen24414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24415" type="x-p"/> I. Here is, The impudent impious brand which the scribes fastened upon Christ's casting out devils, that they might evade and invalidate the conviction of it, and have a poor excuse for not yielding to it. These <hi type="italic">scribes came down from Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.3.22">v. 22</reference>. It should seem they came this long journey on purpose to hinder the progress of the doctrine of Christ; such pains did they take to do mischief; and, coming from Jerusalem, where were the most polite and learned scribes, and where they had opportunity of <hi type="italic">consulting</hi> together <hi type="italic">against the Lord and his Anointed,</hi> they were in the greater capacity to do mischief; the reputation of scribes from Jerusalem would have an influence not only upon the <hi type="italic">country people,</hi> but upon the <hi type="italic">country scribes;</hi> they had never thought of this base suggestion concerning Christ's miracles till the <hi type="italic">scribes from</hi> Jerusalem put it into their heads. They could not deny but that he cast out devils, which plainly bespoke him sent of God; but they insinuated that <hi type="italic">he had Beelzebub</hi> on his side, was in league with him, and by <hi type="italic">the prince of the devils cast out devils.</hi> There is a trick in the case; Satan is not <hi type="italic">cast out,</hi> he only <hi type="italic">goes out</hi> by consent. There was nothing in the manner of Christ's <hi type="italic">casting out devils,</hi> that gave any cause to suspect this; he did it <hi type="italic">as one having authority;</hi> but so they will have it, who resolve not to believe him. <div eID="gen24415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24416" type="x-p"/> II. The rational answer which Christ gave to this objection, demonstrating the absurdity of it. <div eID="gen24416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24417" type="x-p"/> 1. Satan is so <hi type="italic">subtle,</hi> that he will never voluntarily quit his possession; <hi type="italic">If Satan cast out Satan, his kingdom is divided against itself,</hi> and it <hi type="italic">cannot stand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.3.23-Mark.3.26">v. 23-26</reference>. He <hi type="italic">called them to him,</hi> as one desirous they should be convinced; he treated them with all the freedom, friendliness, and familiarity that could be; he vouchsafed to reason the case with them, <hi type="italic">that every mouth may be stopped.</hi> It was plain that the doctrine of Christ <hi type="italic">made war</hi> upon the devil's kingdom, and had a direct tendency to break his power, and crush his interest in the souls of men; and it was as plain that the casting of him out of the bodies of people confirmed that doctrine, and gave it the setting on; and therefore it cannot be imagined that he should come into such a design; every one knows that Satan is no <hi type="italic">fool,</hi> nor will act so directly against his own interest. <div eID="gen24417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24418" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ is so <hi type="italic">wise,</hi> that, being engaged in war with him, he will attack his forces wherever he meets them, whether in the bodies or souls of people, <reference osisRef="Mark.3.27">v. 27</reference>. It is plain, Christ's design is to <hi type="italic">enter into the strong man's house,</hi> to take possession of the interest he has in the world, and to <hi type="italic">spoil his goods,</hi> and convert them to his own service; and therefore it is natural to suppose that he will thus <hi type="italic">bind the strong man,</hi> will forbid him to <hi type="italic">speak</hi> when he would, and to <hi type="italic">stay</hi> where he would, and thus show that he has gained a victory over him. <div eID="gen24418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24419" type="x-p"/> III. The awful warning Christ gave them to take heed how they spoke such dangerous words as these; however they might make light of them, as only conjectures, and the language of <hi type="italic">free-thinking,</hi> if they persisted in it, it would be of fatal consequence to them; it would be found a sin against the last remedy, and consequently <hi type="italic">unpardonable;</hi> for what could be imagined possible to bring <hi type="italic">them</hi> to repentance for their sin in blaspheming Christ, who would set aside such a <hi type="italic">strong</hi> conviction with such a <hi type="italic">weak</hi> evasion? It is true, the gospel <hi type="italic">promiseth,</hi> because Christ hath <hi type="italic">purchased,</hi> forgiveness for the greatest sins and sinners, <reference osisRef="Mark.3.28">v. 28</reference>. Many of those who reviled Christ on the cross (which was a <hi type="italic">blaspheming of the Son of man,</hi> aggravated to the highest degree), found mercy, and Christ himself prayed, <hi type="italic">Father, forgive them;</hi> but this was <hi type="italic">blaspheming the Holy Ghost,</hi> for it was by the Holy Spirit that he <hi type="italic">cast out</hi> devils, and they said, It was <hi type="italic">by the unclean spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.3.30">v. 30</reference>. By this method they would outface the conviction of all the gifts of the Holy Ghost after Christ's ascension, and defeat them all, after which there remained no more proof, and therefore they should <hi type="italic">never have forgiveness,</hi> but were <hi type="italic">liable to eternal damnation.</hi> They were in imminent danger of that everlasting punishment, from which there was <hi type="italic">no redemption,</hi> and in which there was no <hi type="italic">intermission,</hi> no <hi type="italic">remission.</hi>
entries.7beb346f018f0a6ae768f5973d67a0f7901057c8: <div eID="gen24419" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Family of Christ.</title> <div sID="gen24420" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> There came then his brethren and his mother, and, standing without, sent unto him, calling him. <hi type="super">32</hi> And the multitude sat about him, and they said unto him, Behold, thy mother and thy brethren without seek for thee. <hi type="super">33</hi> And he answered them, saying, Who is my mother, or my brethren? <hi type="super">34</hi> And he looked round about on them which sat about him, and said, Behold my mother and my brethren! <hi type="super">35</hi> For whosoever shall do the will of God, the same is my brother, and my sister, and mother. <div eID="gen24420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24421" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The <hi type="italic">disrespect</hi> which Christ's <hi type="italic">kindred, according to the flesh,</hi> showed to him, when he was preaching (and they knew very well that he was then in his element); they not only <hi type="italic">stood without,</hi> having no desire to come in, and hear him, but they sent in a message to <hi type="italic">call him out to them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.31-Mark.3.32">v. 31, 32</reference>), as if he must leave his work, to hearken to their <hi type="italic">impertinences;</hi> it is probable that they had <hi type="italic">no business with him,</hi> only sent for him on purpose to oblige him to <hi type="italic">break off,</hi> lest he should <hi type="italic">kill himself.</hi> He knew how far his strength would go, and preferred the salvation of souls before his own life, and soon after made it to appear with a witness; it was therefore an <hi type="italic">idle thing</hi> for them, under pretence of his sparing himself, to interrupt him; and it was worse, if really they had business with him, when they knew he preferred his business, as a Saviour, so much before any other business. <div eID="gen24421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24422" type="x-p"/> 2. The <hi type="italic">respect</hi> which Christ showed to his spiritual kindred upon this occasion. Now, as at other times, he put a <hi type="italic">comparative neglect</hi> upon his mother, which seemed purposely designed to obviate the prevent the extravagant respect which men in aftertimes would be apt to pay her. <hi type="italic">Our</hi> respect ought to be guided and governed by Christ's; now the virgin Mary, or Christ's mother, is not equalled with, but postponed to, ordinary believers, on whom Christ here puts a <hi type="italic">superlative</hi> honour. He looked upon those that <hi type="italic">at about</hi> him, and pronounced those of them that not only heard, but did, the will of God, to be to him as <hi type="italic">his brother, and sister, and mother;</hi> as much esteemed, loved, and cared for, as his nearest relations, <reference osisRef="Mark.3.33-Mark.3.35">v. 33-35</reference>. This is a good reason why we should <hi type="italic">honour those that fear the Lord,</hi> and choose them for our people; why we should be not hearers of the word only, but doers of the work, that we may share with the saints in this honour, Surely it is good to be akin to those who are thus nearly allied to Christ, and to have fellowship with those that have fellowship with Christ; and woe to those that hate and persecute Christ's kindred, that are <hi type="italic">his bone and his flesh,</hi> every one <hi type="italic">resembling the children of a king</hi> (see <reference osisRef="Judg.8.18-Judg.8.19">Judg. viii. 18, 19</reference>); for he will with jealously plead their cause, and avenge their blood.  <chapter eID="Mark.3"/> <div eID="gen24422" type="x-p"/>

entries.de77409db43de129be7d43cf811ba8ff2fe4e3fb: <div eID="gen39171" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen39172" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39173" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39173" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39172" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39174" type="x-p"/> The man with the withered hand healed, <reference osisRef="Mar.3.1-Mar.3.5">Mar 3:1-5</reference>. The Pharisees plot our Lord's destruction, <reference osisRef="Mar.3.6">Mar 3:6</reference>. Christ withdraws, and is followed by a great multitude, <reference osisRef="Mar.3.7-Mar.3.9">Mar 3:7-9</reference>. He heals many, and goes to a mountain to pray, <reference osisRef="Mar.3.10-Mar.3.13">Mar 3:10-13</reference>. He ordains twelve disciples, and, gives them power to preach and work miracles, <reference osisRef="Mar.3.14">Mar 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.3.15">Mar 3:15</reference>. Their names, <reference osisRef="Mar.3.16-Mar.3.19">Mar 3:16-19</reference>. The multitudes throng him, and the scribes attribute his miracles to Beelzebub, <reference osisRef="Mar.3.20-Mar.3.22">Mar 3:20-22</reference>. He vindicates himself by a parable, <reference osisRef="Mar.3.23-Mar.3.27">Mar 3:23-27</reference>. Of the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost, <reference osisRef="Mar.3.28-Mar.3.30">Mar 3:28-30</reference>. His mother and brethren send for him, <reference osisRef="Mar.3.31">Mar 3:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.3.32">Mar 3:32</reference>. And he takes occasion from this to show, that they who do the will of God are to him as his brother, sister, and mother, <reference osisRef="Mar.3.33-Mar.3.35">Mar 3:33-35</reference>. <div eID="gen39174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39175" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen39175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39176" type="x-p"/> A man there which had a withered hand - See this explained on <reference osisRef="Mat.12.10">Mat 12:10</reference> (note), etc., and on <reference osisRef="Luk.6.6">Luk 6:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.6.10">Luk 6:10</reference> (note).
entries.b8c83658933f3db5afceaf3546271e22c06831fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen39176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39177" type="x-p"/> They watched him - Παρετηρουν αυτον, they maliciously watched him. See on <reference osisRef="Luk.14.1">Luk 14:1</reference> (note).
entries.174ce8f5910e0df43cfb9018cd0007a65bd35e5f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen39177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39178" type="x-p"/> To do good - or - evil? to save life, or to kill? - It was a maxim with the Jews, as it should be with all men, that he who neglected to preserve life when it was in his power, was to be reputed a murderer. Every principle of sound justice requires that he should be considered in this light. But, if this be the case, how many murderers are there against whom there is no law but the law of God! <div eID="gen39178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39179" type="x-p"/> To kill - but instead of αποκτειναι, several MSS. and versions have απολεσαι to destroy. Wetstein and Griesbach quote Theophylact for this reading; but it is not in my copy. Paris edit. 1635.
entries.24185a57dd79027371a6b49edbfbcb125e89364f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen39179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39180" type="x-p"/> With anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts - These words are not found in any of the other evangelists. For πωρωσει hardness, or rather callousness, the Codex Bezae, and four of the Itala, read νεκρωσει, deadness; the Vulgate and some of the Itala, caecitate, blindness. Join all these together, and they will scarcely express the fullness of this people's wretchedness. By a long resistance to the grace and Spirit of God, their hearts had become callous; they were past feeling. By a long opposition to the light of God, they became dark in their understanding, were blinded by the deceitfulness of sin, and thus were past seeing. By a long continuance in the practice of every evil work, they were cut off from all union with God, the fountain of spiritual life; and, becoming dead in trespasses and sins, they were incapable of any resurrection but through a miraculous power of God. <div eID="gen39180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39181" type="x-p"/> With anger. What was the anger which our Lord felt? That which proceeded from excessive grief, which was occasioned by their obstinate stupidity and blindness: therefore it was no uneasy passion, but an excess of generous grief. <div eID="gen39181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39182" type="x-p"/> Whole as the other - This is omitted by the best MSS. and versions. <div eID="gen39182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39183" type="x-p"/> Grotius, Mill, and Bengel approve of the omission, and Griesbach leaves it out of the text.
entries.c344990b856c7d58b24d94fb01b74fb6b03d0715: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen39183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39184" type="x-p"/> Herodians - For an account of these, see the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.16.1">Mat 16:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mat.22.16">Mat 22:16</reference>.
entries.0265f211425dca39c593755e9b33fef40b4f0209: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen39184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39185" type="x-p"/> Galilee - See <reference osisRef="Mat.4.13">Mat 4:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.4.15">Mat 4:15</reference>.
entries.110445682991b2a9dd0dda5ceb84c4feb7fef61e: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen39185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39186" type="x-p"/> Tyre - Sidon, etc. - See <reference osisRef="Mat.11.21">Mat 11:21</reference>. <div eID="gen39186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39187" type="x-p"/> When they had heard what great things he did, came unto him - So, if Christ be persecuted and abandoned by the wicked, there are a multitude of pious souls who earnestly seek and follow him. He who labors for God will always find more than he loses, in the midst of all his contradictions and persecutions.
entries.7fe5f9c134231a8043b93144cc862965f56f3490: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen39187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39188" type="x-p"/> A small ship - Πλοιαριον. The lytil boot, Old English MS. It was doubtless something of the boat kind, which probably belonged to some of the disciples. Our Lord was at this time teaching by the sea of Galilee. The word ship is utterly improper in many places of our translation, and tends to mislead the people.
entries.e36c8ade9322438e1e9e2ed153dea53690b46ff4: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen39188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39189" type="x-p"/> They pressed upon him - Rushed upon him, επιπιπτειν - through eagerness to have their spiritual and bodily maladies immediately removed. <div eID="gen39189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39190" type="x-p"/> Plagues - Rather disorders, μαϚιγας; properly such disorders as were inflicted by the Lord. The word plague also tends to mislead.
entries.69776302d57e8e1a5d6d86a7179f7a1301d7552d: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen39190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39191" type="x-p"/> Thou art the Son of God - Two MSS., and the later Syriac, have, Thou art the Christ, the Son of God. One of Stephens's MSS. has, Thou art the Holy One of God. A MS. in the library of Leicester has, συ ει ὁ Θεος, υἱος, Thou art God, the Son. This is an uncommon reading, which is not confirmed by any MS. yet discovered.
entries.00f4f79b466e7e2c1273ff0df4d117dea20949c3: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen39191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39192" type="x-p"/> He ordained twelve - Εποιησε, he made twelve. Here is nothing of what we call ordaining. Christ simply appointed them to be with him; and that he might send them occasionally to preach, etc. <div eID="gen39192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39193" type="x-p"/> To preach - The Codex Bezae, Saxon, and all the Itala, except one, add το ευαγγελιον, the Gospel.
entries.1ece2253d3c8ab11dc2d0cb436c9cadd0dbb9b29: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen39193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39194" type="x-p"/> To have power to heal - and to cast out devils - The business of a minister of Christ is, 1st. To preach the Gospel. 2dly. To be the physician of souls. And, 3dly. To wage war with the devil, and destroy his kingdom.
entries.a93cf26b452ba4eb618332811ff4baccb374b859: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen39194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39195" type="x-p"/> Simon, etc. - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.10.2">Mat 10:2</reference> (note), etc.
entries.c90dfaaa5bc07a437a0293b74bf953f2bc8faba2: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen39195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39196" type="x-p"/> Sons of thunder - A Hebraism for thunderers; probably so named because of their zeal and power in preaching the Gospel. <div eID="gen39196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39197" type="x-p"/> The term Boanerges is neither Hebrew nor Syriac. Calmet and others think that there is reason to believe that the Greek transcribers have not copied it exactly. בני רעם beney raam, which the ancient Greeks would pronounce Beneregem, and which means sons of thunder, was probably the appellative used by our Lord: or בני רעש beni reges, sons of tempest, which comes nearest to the Boanerges of the evangelist. St. Jerome, on Daniel 1, gives בני רעם (which he writes Benereem, softening the sound of the ע ain) as the more likely reading, and Luther, supposing our Lord spoke in Hebrew, gives the proper Hebrew term above mentioned, which he writes Bnehargem. Some think that the reason why our Lord gave this appellative to the sons of Zebedee was, their desire to bring fire down from heaven, i.e. a storm of thunder and lightning, to overturn and consume a certain Samaritan village, the inhabitants of which would not receive their Master. See the account in <reference osisRef="Luk.9.53">Luk 9:53</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.54">Luk 9:54</reference> (note). It was a very usual thing among the Jews to give surnames, which signified some particular quality or excellence, to their rabbins. See several instances in Schoettgen.
entries.f79c1710604af5caa8d7ec17be80d3df1dc96519: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen39197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39198" type="x-p"/> Into a house - As Christ was now returned to Capernaum, this was probably the house of Peter, mentioned <reference osisRef="Mar.2.1">Mar 2:1</reference>.
entries.eb337873d450a4186fcd86e49d800bcffb25d4a1: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen39198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39199" type="x-p"/> Eat bread - Had no time to take any necessary refreshment.
entries.5c92bb39cc531e0353d4c4b7a096c4244367e28a: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen39199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39200" type="x-p"/> His friends - Or, relations. On this verse several MSS. differ considerably. I have followed the reading of the Syriac, because I think it the best: οἱ παρ' αυτου signify merely his relatives, his brethren, etc., see <reference osisRef="Mar.3.31">Mar 3:31</reference>; and the phrase is used by the best writers to signify relatives, companions, and domestics. See Kypke in loc. <div eID="gen39200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39201" type="x-p"/> They said, He is beside himself - It was the enemies of Christ that raised this report; and his relatives, probably thinking that it was true, went to confine him. Let a Christian but neglect the care of his body for a time, in striving to enter in at the strait gate; let a minister of Christ but impair his health by his pastoral labors; presently "he is distracted;" he has "not the least conduct nor discretion." entries.9f4316ab80e4e4e058ce2acc5430c12e246a6541:
Verse 4. Or to do evil? to saw life, or to kill?. It seems to have been a maxim with the Jews, that not to do good, when we have an opportunity, was to do evil; not to save life was to kill, or to be guilty of murder. If a man has an opportunity of saving a man's life when he is in danger, and does not do it, he is evidently guilty of his death. On this principle our Saviour puts this question to the Jews, whether it was better for him, having the power to heal this man, to do it, or to suffer him to remain in this suffering condition. And he illustrates it by an example, showing that in a matter of much less importance--that respecting their cattle--they would do on the Sabbath just as he would if he should heal this man. The same remark may apply to all opportunities of doing good. "The ability to do good imposes an obligation to do it."--Cotton Mather. He that has the means of feeding the hungry, and clothing the naked, and instructing the ignorant, and sending the gospel to the destitute, and that does it not, is guilty; for he is practically doing evil; he is suffering evils to exist which he might remove, So the wicked will be condemned in the day of judgment, because "they did it not," Mt 25:45. If this be true, what an obligation rests on the rich to do good!

(c) "to save life" Hos 6:6
entries.f409871d7cb17e5cebf1fc16d5c66f8ad76fb370:
Verse 5. With anger. With a severe and stern countenance; with indignation at their hypocrisy and hardness of heart. This was not, however, a spiteful or revengeful passion; it was caused by excessive grief at their state. It was not sudden and tumultuous hatred of the men whose hearts were so hard; it was hatred of the sin which they exhibited, joined with the extreme grief that neither his teaching, nor the law of God, nor any means which could be used, overcame their confirmed wickedness. Such anger is not unlawful, Eph 4:26. And, in this instance, our Lord has taught us that anger is never lawful, except when it is tempered with grief or compassion for those who have offended.

Hardness of their hearts. The heart--figuratively the seat of feeling, or affection is said to be tender when it is easily affected by the sufferings of others; by our own sin and danger; by the love and commands of God;--when we are easily made to feel on the great subjects pertaining to our interest, Eze 11:19,20. It is hard, when nothing moves it; when a man is alike insensible to the sufferings of others, the dangers of his own condition, and the commands, the love, and the threatenings of God. It is most tender in youth, or when we have committed fewest crimes. It is made hard by indulgence in sin; by long resisting the offers of life; or by opposing any great and affecting appeals which God may make to us by his Spirit or Providence, by affliction, or by a revival of religion. Hence it is that the most favourable period for securing an interest in Christ, or for becoming a Christian, is in youth; the first, the tenderest, and the best days of life. Nay, in the days of childhood--in the Sabbath-school--God may be found, and the soul prepared to die.

entries.c87b6eed539e1924e3507b7f5c8dd8ebef783e71:

They therefore determined to remove him, if possible, and thus avoid his reproofs. Sinners would often rather put to death the man that reproves them, than to forsake their sins. entries.b7bdfa0b561c421eb11106dc93786da4acdc68c6:
Verses 7,8. To the sea. The sea of Galilee. Or, to the desert and lonely regions which surrounded the sea, where he might be in obscurity, and avoid their designs against his life. His time had not yet come, and he prudently took care of his life; thus showing that we are not needlessly to throw ourselves into danger.

Galilee. See Mt 2:22.

Judea. See Mt 2:1.

Jerusalem. Jerusalem was in Judaea. It is mentioned particularly to show that not only the people of the surrounding country came, but also many from the capital, the place of wealth, and honour, and power.

Idumaea. The country formerly inhabited by the Edomites; in the time of the Saviour, the most southern part of the land of Canaan. The word Idumaea is a Greek word, made from the Hebrew Edom. It signifies the land of Edom, a name given to Esau, one of the sons of Isaac, Gen 25:30. The word signifies red, and was given to him because he sought of Jacob red pottage, as the price of his birthright. He settled in Mount Seir, (De 2:6,) on the south of the land of Canaan, and the country of Idumaea was bounded by Palestine on the north. During the Babylonish captivity, the Edomites spread themselves into the country of Judaea, and occupied a considerable part of the south of Palestine. They had, however, submitted to the rite of circumcision, and were incorporated with the Jews. From them sprang Herod the Great.

From beyond Jordan. From the east coast of the river Jordan. The sacred writers lived on the west side of Jordan ; and by the country beyond Jordan, they meant that on the east side.

Tyre and Sidon. Mt 11:21.

entries.3bae3bd0ac5f08badda99b842fef84b0f76d748f:
Verse 9. A small ship. Rather, a boat. There were, properly speaking; no ships on the sea of Tiberias. This was probably a small boat that belonged to his disciples, in which he could sit, off from the shore, and teach the people, without being pressed by them.

Lest they should throng him. They pressed upon him in great numbers. He had healed many; and those who were still diseased pressed or crowded on him, so as to endanger his life. He therefore withdrew from the multitude, and sought a situation where he might be free from danger.

As many as had plagues. As many as had diseases, or maladies of body or mind. The word plague, now confined to the pestilence, does not express the meaning of the original, and tends to mislead.

entries.4d3545dc0e4aeedca4392223aa678d135a0cdfa3:
Verses 11,12. Unclean spirits. Persons who were possessed of evil spirits.

Thou art the Son of God. The Son of God, by way of eminence. In this place it is equivalent to the Messiah, who was, among the Jews, called the Son of God. Hence they were charged not to make him known, because he was not desirous that it should be blazoned abroad that he claimed to be the Messiah. He had not yet done what he wished to establish his claims to the Messiahship; he was poor and unhonoured, and the claim would be treated as that of an impostor, as it was afterwards, and would endanger his life. For the present, therefore, he did not wish that it should be proclaimed abroad that he was the Messiah.

This circumstance proves the existence of evil spirits. If these were merely diseased or deranged persons, then it is strange that they should be endowed with knowledge so much superior to those in health. If they were under the influence of an order of spirits superior to man--whose appropriate habitation was in another world--then it is not strange that they should know him, even in the midst of his poverty, to be the Messiah, the Son of God.

entries.2c0ad2d6e9d595efdc2485f09df9d74151054a61:
Verse 14. He ordained twelve. The word rendered ordained, here, does not express our notion of ordination to the ministry. It means, literally, "he made," or he appointed twelve to be with him.

Twelve. The reason why twelve were chosen was, probably, that such a number would be deemed competent witnesses of what they saw; that so many could not be supposed to be imposed upon; that they could not be easily charged with being excited by sympathy, or being deluded, as a multitude might; and that, being destined to go into all the world, a considerable number seemed indispensable. Perhaps, also, there was some reference to the fact that twelve was the number of the tribes of Israel.
entries.aeb214279c0ac778a186b4b39319003d2eef8c25:

Some suppose it was because they wished to call down fire from heaven, and consume a certain village of the Samaritans, Lk 9:54. entries.6c6275c118a76bf18585c10b7653121a64f76a24:
Verse 20. They could not so much as eat bread. Their time and attention were so occupied, that they were obliged to forego their regular meals. The affairs of religion may so occupy the attention of ministers, and others, as to destroy their relish for the ordinary comforts and employments of life, and prevent their engaging in their customary pursuits. Religion is all-important--far more important than the ordinary business of this life; and there is nothing unreasonable if our temporal affairs sometimes give way to the higher interests of our own souls, and the souls of others. At the same time, it is true that religion is ordinarily consistent with a close attention to worldly business, It promotes industry, economy, order, neatness, and punctuality--all indispensable to worldly prosperity. Of these there has been no more illustrious example than that of our Saviour himself.

(o) "so that they" Mk 6:31
entries.0482c176e0168a6a943c3a3fd97ee79b7f00f6fc:
Verse 21. When his friends. Greek, "They who were of him." Not the apostles, but his relatives, his friends, who were in the place of his nativity.

Heard of it. Heard of his conduct; his preaching; his appointing the apostles; his drawing such a multitude to his preaching. This shows, that by "his friends" were not meant the apostles, but those at a distance who heard of his conduct.

They went out to lay hold on him. To take him away from the multitude, and to remove him to his home, that he might be treated as a maniac, and, by absence from the causes of excitement, might be restored to his right mind.

They said. That is, common report said. Or, his friends said, for they did not believe on him, Jn 7:5. Probably the enemies of Jesus raised the report, and his relatives were persuaded to believe it to be true.

He is beside himself. He is delirious, or deranged, The reason why this report gained any belief was, probably, that our Lord had lived among them as a carpenter; that he was poor, and unknown; and that now, at thirty years of age, he broke off from his occupations, abandoned his common employment, spent much time in the deserts, denied himself the common comforts of life, and set up his claims to be the Messiah, who was expected by all the people to come with great pomp and splendour. The charge of derangement on account of attention to religion has not been confined to our Saviour. Let a man be made deeply sensible of his sins, and spend much of his time in prayer, and have no relish for the ordinary amusements or business of life; or let a Christian be much impressed with his obligation to devote himself to God, and act as if he believed there was an eternity, and warn his neighbours of their danger; or let a minister show uncommon zeal, and waste his strength in the service of his Master, and the world is not slow to call it derangement. And none will be more ready to originate or believe the charge than an ungodly and infidel parent or brother; a self-righteous Pharisee or professor in the church. At the same time, men may endanger themselves on the bosom of the deep, or in the bowels of the earth, for wealth; or may plunge into the vortex of fashion, and folly, and vice, and break in upon the hours of repose, and neglect their duties to their family, and the demands of business, and in the view of the world it is wisdom, and proof of a sane mind! Such is the consistency of boasted reason; such the wisdom and prudence of worldly men!

Mark 3:5. And when he had looked around upon them with indignation To convince us that this was a just and holy anger, Mark explains the reason of it to be, that he was grieved on account of the blindness of their hearts. First, then, Christ is grieved, because men who have been instructed in the Law of God are so grossly blind; but as it was malice that blinded them, his grief is accompanied by indignation. This is the true moderation of zeal, to be distressed about the destruction of wicked men, and, at the same time, to be filled with wrath at their ungodliness. Again, as this passage assures us, that Christ was not free from human passions, we infer from it, that the passions themselves are not sinful, provided there be no excess. In consequence of the corruption of our nature, we do not preserve moderation; and our anger, even when it rests on proper grounds, is never free from sin. With Christ the case was different; for not only did his nature retain its original purity, but he was a perfect pattern of righteousness. We ought therefore to implore from heaven the Spirit of God to correct our excesses.

entries.42bae34829af08a8b7d14aa8280b5ada7d6ece04: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.3.6" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.3.6" sID="gen98835" type="section"/> <div sID="gen98836" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.3.6">Mark 3:6</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">The Pharisees took counsel with the Herodians. </hi>Now they regarded <hi type="italic">the Herodians </hi>with the fiercest hatred; for their eagerness to be considered the guardians and protectors of public liberty made it necessary for them to make an open profession of mortal hatred to the ministers of that tyrant. And yet this aversion is counteracted by their hatred and fury against Christ, <note n="88"> <div sID="gen98837" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Toutesfois la haine enragee qu’ils ont contre Christ, surmonte toutes leurs autres meschantes affections</foreign>;” — “and yet the enraged hatred which they have against Christ rises above all their other wicked dispositions.”<div eID="gen98837" type="x-p"/> </note> which makes them not only enter into a conspiracy with foreigners, but insinuate themselves into the good graces of those with whom, on other occasions, they would have shrunk from intercourse. While ungodliness hurries men in various directions, and drives them to different courses, it engages them, with one consent, in a contest with God. No hostilities prevent them from giving their hand to each other for opposing the truth of God.<div eID="gen98836" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.3.6" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen98835" osisID="Mark.3.6" type="section"/>
entries.57d2c0cef1eb8518aa58364acbb5e078a18210eb: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.3.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.3.13" sID="gen97043" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97044" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.3.13">Mark 3:13</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And he went up into a mountain.</hi> By this election he does not yet ordain them to be <hi type="italic">Apostles, </hi>to enter immediately into the discharge of their office, but merely admits them to enjoy his private instructions <note n="348"> <div sID="gen97045" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pour ses disciples et escoliers domestiques</foreign>;” — “for his disciples and private scholars.”<div eID="gen97045" type="x-p"/> </note> with a view to the apostleship. Commentators have fallen into a mistake here, by confounding those passages with the tenth chapter of the Gospel by Matthew. For the plain meaning of the words is, that they are only destined to a future commission, the bestowal of which is recorded by Matthew; and Mark and Luke will be found afterwards relating, in its proper place, the mission which Matthew there describes. And we need not wonder, if their heavenly Master chose to train and accustom them gradually to so arduous an employment: for, even by a long course of instruction, their ignorance could not be corrected.<div eID="gen97044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen97046" type="x-p"/>Both the Evangelists say, that Christ <hi type="italic">went up into a mountain. </hi>Luke explains the cause to have been, that he might <hi type="italic">pray </hi>with greater freedom in his retirement, which he was accustomed to do frequently, as is evident from other passages. Now, this example ought to be regarded by us as a perpetual rule, to begin with prayer, when we are about to choose pastors to churches: otherwise, what we attempt will not succeed well. And certainly our <hi type="italic">Lord </hi>prayed, not so much on his own account, as to lay down a rule for us. We are deficient in prudence and skill; and though our sagacity were of the highest order, nothing is more easy than to be deceived in this matter. Granting that we were in no danger of mistake, if the Lord does not regulate our affections, with what force, or rather violence, shall we be carried away <note n="349"> <div sID="gen97047" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Destournez et transportez hors du droit chemin</foreign>;” — “turned and carried away out of the right road.”<div eID="gen97047" type="x-p"/> </note> by favor and prepossession, or hatred or ambition? Besides, though the election were conducted in the very best manner, all will be unsuccessful, unless the Lord take under his guidance those who are elected, and furnish them with the necessary gifts. “What then?” it will be said, “did not Christ earnestly implore the Father to preside in the election?” This I readily acknowledge, and I have also to state, that this was a declaration and acknowledgment of his care for his Church. Accordingly, he did not pray to the Father in the ordinary manner, but <hi type="italic">spent the whole night in prayer. </hi>But if he, who was full of the Holy Spirit, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.3.34">John 3:34</reference>,) implored the Father, with such ardor and earnestness, to preside in the election, how much greater need have we to do so?<div eID="gen97046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen97048" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">He called to him whom he would.</hi> By this expression, I have no doubt, Mark conveys to us the instruction, that it was to the unmixed grace of Christ, and not to any excellence of their own, that they were indebted for receiving so honorable an office: for, if you understand him to say, that those were chosen, who were more excellent than others, this will not apply to Judas. The meaning, therefore, is the apostle-ship was not bestowed on account of any human merits; but, by the free mercy of God, persons, who were altogether unworthy of it, were raised to that high rank; and thus was fulfilled what Christ says on another occasion, <hi type="italic">“Ye </hi>have not chosen me, but I have chosen you,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.15.16">John 15:16</reference>.) To the same effect Paul frequently speaks, extolling the purpose of God in bestowing on him the apostleship, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.3.7">Ephesians 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Col.1.25">Colossians 1:25</reference>.)<div eID="gen97048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen97049" type="x-p"/>But here many questions arise. <hi type="italic">First</hi>, why did our Lord deliberately choose Judas, who, he perfectly knew, was unworthy of the honor, and would be his betrayer? <hi type="italic">Secondly</hi>, why did God, after being so earnestly supplicated by his Son, and as if he had given a refusal to Christ, permit a base and wicked man to find his way to the highest rank in his Church? <note n="350"> <div sID="gen97050" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pourquoy Dieu estant prie et requis si ardemment par son Fils, asouffert qu'un mechant et mal-heureux traitre fust eleve au rang le plus honorable de son Eglise, comme si Jesus Christ n'eust point este exauce</foreign>?” — “Why did God, when entreated and requested so earnestly by his Son, permit a wicked and unhappy traitor to be elevated to the most honorable rank in his Church, as if Jesus Christ had not been listened to?”<div eID="gen97050" type="x-p"/> </note> <hi type="italic">Thirdly</hi>, why did he resolve that the first-fruits <note n="351"> <div sID="gen97051" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Les premices et premier commencement de son Eglise</foreign>;” — “the first-fruits and first beginning of his Church.”<div eID="gen97051" type="x-p"/> </note> of his Church should be stained by so foul a disgrace? <hi type="italic">Fourthly</hi>, how came it, that Jesus Christ, knowingly and willingly, preferred Judas to honest and faithful ministers?<div eID="gen97049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen97052" type="x-p"/>The first objection is met by the following reply. Our Lord expressly intended to prevent future offenses, that we may not feel excessive uneasiness, when unprincipled men occupy the situation of teachers in the Church, or when professors of the Gospel become apostates. He gave, at the same time, in the person of one man, an instance of fearful defection, <note n="352"> <div sID="gen97053" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Un revoltement et cheute horrible</foreign>;” — “a dreadful rebellion and fall.”<div eID="gen97053" type="x-p"/> </note> that those who occupy a higher rank may not indulge in self-complacency. At the same time, with regard to the second question, we do not admit that our Lord suffered a refusal. <note n="353"> <div sID="gen97054" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Cependant nous ne dirons pas que Christ a este esconduit, veu que le pere par un conseil admirable, mettant un diable en la compagnie d’onze Anges, a toutesfois tellement modere l’issue, que la cheute de cestuy-la a plustost conferme que non pas esbranle la foyde son Eglise</foreign>.” — “Yet we will not say that Christ was refused, since the Father, by a wonderful purpose, putting a devil into the company of eleven angels, has, at the same time, so guided the result, that the fall of this man, instead of shaking, has rather confirmed, the faith of his Church.”<div eID="gen97054" type="x-p"/> </note> This answer will serve also for the third question. At the very beginning, it was judged proper to give an early demonstration of the future state of the Church, that weak persons might not stumble on account of the fall of a reprobate; for it is not proper, that the stability of the Church should depend on men. With regard to the last objection, Christ did not prefer Judas to devout and holy disciples, but raised him to an eminence from which he was afterwards to fall, and thus intended to make him an example and instruction to men of every condition and of every age, that no one may abuse the honor which God has conferred upon him, and likewise that, when even the pillars fall, those who appear to be the weakest of believers may remain steady.<div eID="gen97052" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.3.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97043" osisID="Mark.3.13" type="section"/>

Mark 3:16. And to Simon he gave the name Peter. Though all Christians must be living stones
This alludes to the Greek word Πέτρος, (Peter,) which literally signifies a stone. We shall afterwards find (Matthew 16:18) that our Lord makes express reference to the meaning of the name. — Ed.
, of the spiritual temple, yet Christ gave this name peculiarly to Simon, according to the measure of grace which he intended to bestow upon him. This is not inconsistent with the shameful weakness which he manifested in denying his Lord: for this title showed his invincible power and steadiness, which continued till his death. Yet it is absurd in the Papists to infer from this, that the Church is founded on him, as will afterwards be more fully explained, (Matthew 16:18.) Christ called the sons of Zebedee sons of thunder, because he was to give them a powerful voice, that they might thunder throughout the whole world.
“Afin qu’ils tonnassent par tout le monde en preschant;” — “in order that they might thunder throughout the whole world in preaching.”
And that thunder is heard, in the present day, from the mouth of John. As to his brother, there can be no doubt that, so long as he lived, he shook the earth. The word has been corrupted: for the full pronunciation would be בני רגש, (Benae-regesh;)
Philologists have been a good deal perplexed by this word. There is even some difficulty in settling the Greek orthography: for conflicting manuscripts present us with the various forms of Βοανηργές, Βοανεργής, and Βοανεργείς. The name is unquestionably of Hebrew origin. Some of the derivations, which have been given, are so far-fetched as not to deserve refutation. There is plausibility in Jerome's hypothesis, that it comes from רעם, (Ragam,) thunder. But the substitution of final, ς for μ has never been satisfactorily explained. Admitting that ές or ής, is a Greek termination, the absence of the final and radical Mem (ם) is too violent a supposition. After many trials, scholars are pretty nearly agreed, that they must return to the derivation which is suggested by our author, and which some writers have illustrated and defended by a considerable array of learning. — Ed.
but the changes which words undergo in passing into other languages are well known.

he taught them, saying, 3. Happy are the poor in spirit: for their is the kingdom of heaven. 4. Happy are they who mourn: for they shall receive consolation. 5. Happy are the mmek: for they shall receive the earth by inheritance.

20. And he, lifting up his eyes on the disciples, said, Happy (are ye) poor: for yours is the kingdom of God. 21. Happy are ye who hunger now: for ye shall be satisfied. Happy are ye who weep now: for ye shall laugh. 22. Happy shall ye be when men shall hate you, and shall separate you, and shall load you with reproaches, and shall cast out your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man. 23. Rejoice ye in that day, and leap for joy: for, lo, your reward is great in heaven: for according to these things their fathers did to the prophets. 24. But woe to you (who are) rich: for you have your consolation. 25. Woe to you who are filled: for you shall hunger. entries.f37b2836bf99a685837f735d8ec3264eaa5a19f8: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.3.20" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.3.20" sID="gen98887" type="section"/> <div sID="gen98888" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.3.20">Mark 3:20</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And they come into the house. Mark </hi>undoubtedly takes in a somewhat extended period of time, when he passes from the miracles to that wicked conspiracy which the relatives of Christ formed with each other, to bind him as if he had been a <hi type="italic">madman. Matthew </hi>and <hi type="italic">Luke </hi>mention not more than a single miracle, as having given to the Pharisees an opportunity of slander; but as all the three agree in this last clause which is contained in Mark’s narrative, I have thought it proper to insert it here.<div eID="gen98888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen98889" type="x-p"/>It is wonderful that such wickedness should have been found among the relatives of Christ, who ought to have been the first to aid him in advancing the kingdom of God. When they see that he has already obtained some reputation, their ambition leads them to desire that he should be admired in Jerusalem; for they exhort him to go up to that city,<div eID="gen98889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen98890" type="x-p"/>that he may show himself more openly, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.7.3 Bible:John.7.4">John 7:3,4</reference>.)<div eID="gen98890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen98891" type="x-p"/>But now that they perceive him to be hated on one side by the rulers, exposed on another to numerous slanders, and even despised by the great body of the people--to prevent any injury, or envy, or dishonor, from arising to the whole family, they form the design of <hi type="italic">laying hands on him, </hi>and binding him at home, as if he had been a person who labored under mental derangement; and, as appears from the words of the Evangelist, such was their actual belief.<div eID="gen98891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen98892" type="x-p"/>Hence we learn, first, how great is the blindness of the human mind, in forming such perverse judgments about the glory of God when openly displayed. Certainly, in all that Christ said and did, the power of the Holy Spirit shone magnificently; and if others had not clearly perceived it, how could it be unknown to his relatives, who were intimately acquainted with him? But because Christ’s manner of acting does not please the world, and is so far from gaining its good graces that it exposes him to the resentments of many, they give out that he is deranged. Let us learn, in the second place, that the light of faith does not proceed from flesh and blood, but from heavenly grace, that no man may glory in any thing else than in the regeneration of the Spirit; as Paul tells us,<div eID="gen98892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen98893" type="x-p"/>If any man wishes to be considered to be in Christ, <lb/> let him be a new creature, (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.5.17">2 Corinthians 5:17</reference>.)<div eID="gen98893" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.3.20" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen98887" osisID="Mark.3.20" type="section"/>
